title: Immortal Studies
subtitle: Réti's two-hare king walk and the Saavedra underpromotion.
goals: Walk the king along impossible diagonals
Chase two goals with every move
Win with the most famous underpromotion ever

steps.say: Composed endgame studies are chess distilled to pure idea. First, Richard Réti, 1921: White's king stands OUTSIDE the square of Black's h-pawn, and Black's king guards White's c-pawn. Every engine of common sense says White loses. Réti's discovery: a king moving on the DIAGONAL loses no time — it can chase both goals at once. 'The hunt of two hares': catch the pawn OR promote your own, and Black can only stop one.

steps.prompt: Hopeless, says arithmetic: the h-pawn queens in four, your king needs five. Play Réti's thirteen-move miracle and DRAW — chase both hares!
hints: Move the king DIAGONALLY — g7, f6, e5 — every step both chases the h-pawn and approaches your c-pawn. Black cannot defend both futures.
Kg7! h4 Kf6! Kb6 (else the king catches the pawn via e5-f4) Ke5! — and now h3 is met by Kd6! promoting together with Black. Both hares, one hunter.

line.say: One diagonal step — and suddenly the king threatens BOTH to chase the h-pawn (via f6-g5) and to support c7 (via f6-e7). Black pushes...
Still both hares: f6 eyes g5 (catching the pawn) AND e7 (escorting yours). Black must spend a move stopping the c-pawn...
The miracle square: e5 attacks the h-pawn's future via f4 AND stands one step from d6, where it shields the c-pawn home. Black cannot prevent both...
The king abandons the h-pawn — because now his own pawn queens by force alongside it...
Lockstep — both pawns one square from glory...
The escort takes the last guard post: c8 is secured...

Both sides queen — WITH CHECK for White, no less. Draw agreed: from a position every calculation calls lost. Réti's king walked a path that exists only in chess geometry, where the diagonal costs nothing. The most famous half-point in history.

rejections.say: The straight-line chase — h4! and the pawn simply outruns you: count it, four steps to two... hopeless. Only the DIAGONAL walk chases two goals at once: Kg7!
Kb7! and the pawn falls next move, while the h-pawn runs untouched. The pawn can't save itself — only the two-hare KING walk saves the game: Kg7!

steps.wrongSay: Straight lines lose. Which king step moves toward BOTH pawns at once?
steps.successSay: The Réti maneuver — one diagonal, two hares, half a point from nothing. Every endgame book on Earth opens with what you just played.

steps.say: Now the Saavedra position, 1895 — found by an amateur monk reading a newspaper column, and possibly the most famous single move in study history. White: king and one pawn. Black: a ROOK — and rooks massacre lone pawns. Black's plan is brutal: check forever, and the instant your pawn promotes to a queen, sacrifice the rook for stalemate. Your job: promote anyway. The solution will surprise you on move six.

steps.prompt: Rook versus pawn — and the rook has a stalemate trick loaded. Thirteen moves: escort the pawn, dodge the checks, and find the promotion nobody expects!
hints: Walk the king down the b-file beside your pawn: each rook check gets answered one square lower — until Kc2, when Rd4 sets the stalemate trap: c8=Q?? Rc4+! Qxc4 stalemate!
So DON'T take a queen. Promote to a ROOK: c8=R! — now Ra4 threatens mate tries, and Kb3! double-attacks the rook while threatening Rc1#. Black loses everything.

line.say: The pawn steps up — and the rook's checking machine starts...
Down the ladder — staying beside the pawn, never blocking its path. Note: not Kb7?? when Rd7 pins the pawn forever...
Again one rung lower — the rook keeps checking...
The checks run out — the king attacks the rook. Black plays his trump card: the stalemate trap...

THE SAAVEDRA MOVE. A rook, not a queen! c8=Q?? Rc4+! Qxc4 would be STALEMATE — the buried king on a1 has no moves. The modest rook promotion sidesteps the trap entirely, and now Black's rook is lost: Ra4 is forced...

The quiet killer: the king attacks the a4 rook AND threatens Rc1# — checkmate on the back rank. Black cannot parry both. One pawn beat a full rook, thanks to an underpromotion a Spanish monk spotted in 1895. The most celebrated single move in endgame history — played by you, on your board.

rejections.say: Rd7! — pinning the pawn to your king, and it never promotes: the rook just shuffles on the seventh forever. The king walks DOWN the board beside the pawn, never onto its file's seventh-rank crossfire: c7 first!
Rd6! — the rook pins your pawn sideways against the king, and it never moves again. The winning geometry is exact: push c7 NOW, then ladder the king straight down the b-file, one rung per check.

steps.wrongSay: Pawn first, then walk the check-ladder down — and remember: the promotion at the end is NOT a queen.
steps.successSay: c8=R!! — the Saavedra. You've now played both of the most famous endgame studies ever composed. These two ideas — the diagonal king and the anti-stalemate underpromotion — will win and save real games for you.
